CISA: Ransomware gangs now exploiting critical TeamCity flaw
bleepingcomputer.com · 24 Sep 2026 10:42 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra

In plain words

The U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA says ransomware groups are using a serious weakness in JetBrains TeamCity, a tool companies use to build, test, and release software. An internet-connected TeamCity server that has not been updated can let an outsider take control without logging in, exposing stored information and passwords and potentially changing software that companies distribute. More than 30,000 development teams use TeamCity, so affected organizations should install JetBrains’ updates or limit access to trusted networks immediately.

Summary
CISA says ransomware gangs are now exploiting the critical TeamCity authentication-bypass flaw CVE-2026-63077, which can enable unauthenticated remote command execution. Organizations should immediately patch TeamCity to versions 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3, or restrict access to trusted networks.

CISA has flagged CVE-2026-63077, a critical JetBrains TeamCity vulnerability, as being exploited by ransomware gangs. JetBrains patched the flaw on July 25 in TeamCity On-Premises versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3, and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on August 5. U.S. federal agencies were ordered to secure affected networks within three days.

The flaw allows an unauthenticated person with HTTP(S) access to use the TeamCity agent polling protocol to bypass authentication and run operating-system commands with the TeamCity server process’s privileges. A successful compromise can expose TeamCity data, configurations, and stored credentials, alter server state, and potentially affect build artifacts and downstream software delivery pipelines. Shadowserver tracked just over 160 internet-exposed TeamCity servers still unpatched against the flaw, and JetBrains advised organizations unable to patch immediately to restrict access to trusted networks.

  • A successful compromise can affect more than the TeamCity server itself: it may expose stored credentials, alter build artifacts, and undermine downstream software delivery pipelines.
  • Although the number of exposed unpatched TeamCity servers fell from about 700 to just over 160, the remaining systems are still directly reachable from the internet and vulnerable to attacks.
  • CISA has tagged four TeamCity issues as exploited in the wild since October 2023, and all four have also been used in ransomware attacks.
  • JetBrains advised organizations that cannot patch immediately to limit TeamCity access to trusted networks, providing a temporary risk-reduction measure.
Key Points
  • 01CISA has identified CVE-2026-63077, a critical JetBrains TeamCity flaw, as being exploited by ransomware gangs.
  • 02JetBrains patched the issue on July 25 in TeamCity On-Premises versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3.
  • 03The flaw can allow an unauthenticated person with HTTP(S) access to bypass authentication through the TeamCity agent polling protocol and run operating-system commands with the TeamCity server process’s privileges.
  • 04CISA added CVE-2026-63077 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on August 5 and directed U.S. federal agencies to secure their networks within three days.
  • 05Shadowserver tracked just over 160 internet-exposed TeamCity servers that remained unpatched for CVE-2026-63077, down from roughly 700 after the flaw was patched.

In plain words

Attackers started trying to take over WordPress websites within hours of a newly disclosed serious flaw being fixed. The issue can let an outsider run their own code on a site’s server in certain setups, including by creating harmful files. Website owners using affected WordPress versions should install the available updates quickly and look for signs that their sites may have been altered.

Summary
Attackers began probing and exploiting the critical WordPress CVE-2026-87902 remote-code-execution flaw within hours of its disclosure, using pearcmd.php to write malicious PHP files. Administrators should urgently update to WordPress 7.1.2 or the relevant supported patched release and check systems for compromise.

Attackers began actively targeting the critical WordPress vulnerability CVE-2026-87902 within hours of its public disclosure and patch release. The flaw has a CVSS score of 9.2 and can allow an unauthenticated outsider to run code on a server under specific conditions. The first recorded attempt occurred on September 22, 2026, at 11:49 a.m. UTC, the same day patches were released.

Exploitation requires a WordPress theme with a top-level directory beginning with “page-” and a readable local PHP file on the server. Observed requests used /usr/local/lib/php/pearcmd.php to write attacker-controlled PHP files to locations such as /tmp and /var/tmp, and attempted to load an upload script hosted on GitHub. Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts beginning September 23, while Patchstack reported activity progressing from harmless probing to file-writing attempts. Administrators are advised to update to WordPress 7.1.2, or the corresponding patched versions 7.0.6, 6.9.9, and 6.8.10, and review their sites for malicious activity.

  • Successful compromise requires both a theme directory beginning with "page-" and a readable local PHP file, meaning the flaw is critical but not universally exploitable across all WordPress installations.
  • Observed activity progressed from checking harmless WordPress core files to using pearcmd.php to write attacker-controlled PHP files, showing a rapid shift from probing to attempted site takeover.
  • The first recorded exploitation attempt occurred at 11:49 a.m. UTC on the same day patches were released, highlighting how quickly public patch information was operationalized by attackers.
  • WordPress auto-updates are enabled by default, which Previdian said may limit the number of successful compromises even as mass exploitation attempts continue.

  • 02CVE-2026-87902 has a CVSS score of 9.2 and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server when specific theme and server conditions are met.
  • 03Observed malicious requests used /usr/local/lib/php/pearcmd.php to write PHP files to locations including /tmp and /var/tmp, then attempted to load a PHP upload script hosted on GitHub.
  • 04Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts beginning September 23, 2026, with activity linked to IP addresses in the United States and Indonesia.
  • 05Website administrators are advised to update to WordPress 7.1.2 or the corresponding patched releases 7.0.6, 6.9.9, and 6.8.10 and review their sites for malicious activity.

In plain words

Hackers are now using a known weakness in Roundcube Webmail, a browser-based email service used by thousands of organizations and millions of people. The weakness can let an outsider get past the login screen, run harmful commands against the service’s stored information, and steal data. This matters because more than 523,000 Roundcube systems are visible on the internet, and organizations that have not installed the available update may be exposed.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-48842, a pre-authentication SQL injection flaw in Roundcube Webmail’s virtuser_query plugin that can enable authentication bypass and database data theft. Administrators should update to Roundcube 1.6.16 or 1.7.1 immediately, or disable the affected plugin if patching is not possible.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-48842, a high-severity flaw in Roundcube Webmail that was patched in May. Roundcube is a browser-based IMAP email client used by thousands of services and millions of users, and it is pre-installed with cPanel. The warning came four months after Roundcube released fixes in versions 1.6.16 and 1.7.1.

The issue is a pre-authentication SQL injection in Roundcube’s virtuser_query built-in plugin, which handles database-backed user lookups and email-address mappings. Successful exploitation can allow an attacker without privileges to bypass authentication, run malicious database commands, and steal data from Roundcube’s database without user interaction. Administrators should update their servers or, if they cannot update immediately, disable or remove the virtuser_query plugin; Shadowserver tracks more than 523,000 Roundcube instances exposed to the internet, though it is unknown how many are patched or honeypots.

  • The flaw was patched in May but was reported as actively exploited four months later, underscoring that installing available updates remains important after a fix is released.
  • Organizations that cannot update Roundcube immediately have a specific temporary mitigation: disabling or removing the virtuser_query plugin removes the vulnerable entry point.
  • Roundcube has repeatedly been targeted by both cybercrime and state-backed groups; CISA has recorded 11 Roundcube Webmail vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since May 2022.
  • The large number of internet-exposed Roundcube instances does not directly indicate how many systems remain at risk, because the tracked total may include honeypots and already patched servers.
Key Points
  • 01The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security warned that CVE-2026-48842, a Roundcube Webmail flaw patched in May, is being actively exploited in the wild.
  • 02CVE-2026-48842 is a pre-authentication SQL injection in Roundcube’s virtuser_query plugin that can allow attackers to bypass authentication, execute malicious database commands, and steal database data.
  • 03Roundcube fixed the issue in versions 1.6.16 and 1.7.1 and strongly recommended that users update their servers.
  • 04Administrators unable to update immediately can disable or remove the virtuser_query plugin to eliminate the attack vector.
  • 05Shadowserver tracks more than 523,000 Roundcube instances exposed on the internet, although it is unknown how many are patched or honeypots.

Re-Enabled GitHub Actions Expose Thousands of Repositories to Mini Shai-Hulud
socket.dev · 24 Sep 2026 21:14 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra

In plain words

Two GitHub tools used to automate issue and comment cleanup were previously changed to include harmful code, then temporarily blocked by GitHub. When GitHub made them available again in September 2026 without removing that harmful code, thousands of projects that use the tools by version name could start running it automatically. This matters because these small background tasks may have access to project passwords, private information, and permissions, even though many maintainers may not realize the tools are still in use.

Summary
GitHub re-enabled two GitHub Actions repositories compromised in the May 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud campaign without removing malicious release tags, causing tag-pinned downstream workflows to execute the payload again. Organizations should remove or pin these actions to verified clean commit SHAs and rotate secrets exposed in runs after September 16.

GitHub Actions repositories actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment were compromised during the May 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud campaign and disabled by GitHub on May 19. While they were disabled, downstream workflows failed before running because GitHub Actions could not download the repositories. On September 16, 2026, both repositories became accessible again, but their release tags still pointed to the malicious code introduced on May 18.

Workflows that referenced either action by a version tag, rather than a fixed commit SHA, resumed downloading and running the payload on their next scheduled or event-triggered execution. For issues-helper, GitHub’s dependency graph lists about 15,000 dependent repositories, though the number using mutable tags is unknown. Logs showed the affected action resolving v2.2.1 to malicious code, installing Bun through oven-sh/setup-bun, and running bun run $GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/index.js; the article recommends removing the actions or pinning verified clean commit SHAs, rotating exposed secrets, and reviewing workflow histories for suspicious runs.

  • Disabling the compromised repositories temporarily protected downstream projects because GitHub Actions jobs failed while trying to download the actions, before any workflow steps could run.
  • The incident was reactivated without a new compromise or new malicious code: restoring access to repositories whose tags still pointed to harmful code was sufficient.
  • Affected workflows can run the payload without a maintainer doing anything, because these issue-management automations commonly run daily or when users open issues or pull requests.
  • A sudden change from jobs failing in seconds to completing after several minutes, along with downloads of oven-sh/setup-bun and execution of Bun, can help identify affected workflow runs.
  • Pinning an action to a verified clean full commit SHA prevents a later change to an upstream version tag from changing the code a workflow runs.
Key Points
  • 01The GitHub Actions actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment were compromised during the May 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud campaign and were disabled by GitHub on May 19, 2026.
  • 02Both repositories became accessible again on September 16, 2026 while their release tags still pointed to malicious code introduced on May 18.
  • 03Workflows that reference either action by a mutable version tag resumed downloading and executing the malicious payload when the repositories were re-enabled.
  • 04GitHub’s dependency graph lists about 15,000 dependent repositories for actions-cool/issues-helper, although the number using mutable tag references is unknown.
  • 05The article recommends removing the affected actions or pinning them to verified clean commit SHAs, rotating secrets exposed after September 16, and reviewing workflow histories for suspicious runs.

    In plain words

    A newer version of MacSync, a program that steals information from Mac computers, uses public Apple iCloud calendar entries to receive instructions and download more harmful software. It has been spread through fake apps, free or cracked software, and tricks that tell people to copy and run commands. Mac users could lose browser passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, messages, and other personal files, while the added hidden tool can keep returning after a restart and make security warnings less visible. This shows that even familiar online services and convincing-looking software can be misused to help criminals reach victims.

    Summary
    A new MacSync macOS malware variant uses public iCloud calendar event descriptions to retrieve commands and download fresh payloads, making its delivery chain harder to block. It also adds a Finder-disguised backdoor that persists on systems, suppresses notifications, steals data, and can execute attacker-supplied AppleScript.

    A new variant of the Swift-based MacSync macOS information-stealing malware uses public iCloud calendar events to deliver commands and obtain fresh payloads. MacSync, first seen in April 2025, has recently appeared in ClickFix campaigns disguised as Homebrew and macOS disk-space analyzer tools. Kaspersky says the malware, which was previously derived from the AMOS stealer family, has evolved through added modules.

    In one delivery chain, a downloader retrieves commands hidden after the DESCRIPTION: line of a public iCloud calendar event, passes the data to zsh, and downloads a malware archive from iCloud. The archive contains an app bundle that acts as a dropper and ultimately retrieves MacSync. A new Finder-disguised Objective-C backdoor establishes persistence through a LaunchAgent, .zshrc changes, and global Git hooks, suppresses notifications, can run attacker-provided AppleScript, and can deploy a browser extension or replace a Ledger wallet application. MacSync also targets browser data and saved credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, Telegram data, Keychain files, and system, SSH, AWS, Kubernetes, Git, and shell configuration information.

    • MacSync repurposes public iCloud calendar event descriptions as a command-delivery channel, allowing its downloader to retrieve follow-on instructions and payloads through an Apple service.
    • The malware’s persistence extends beyond a standard startup entry by modifying the user’s .zshrc file and global Git hooks, giving it multiple ways to restart after reboot.
    • The Finder-disguised backdoor terminates macOS notification processes, which is intended to prevent alerts from reaching the user while it operates.
    • The backdoor can deploy a browser extension or replace an installed Ledger wallet application with versions supplied by its command-and-control server.
    Key Points
    • 01MacSync is a Swift-based macOS information-stealing malware first seen in April 2025 that has recently been delivered through ClickFix campaigns disguised as Homebrew and disk-space analysis tools.
    • 02Kaspersky found a MacSync delivery chain in which a downloader retrieves commands from the description of a public iCloud calendar event and downloads a later-stage payload from iCloud.
    • 03The calendar data is passed to the macOS zsh shell, where commands placed after the event's DESCRIPTION: line run and retrieve an archive containing an app bundle that acts as a dropper.
    • 04MacSync's information-stealing component targets browser history, cookies, saved credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, Telegram data, Keychain files, system and device information, and SSH, AWS, Kubernetes, Git, and shell configuration files.
    • 05A new Objective-C backdoor disguised as Finder establishes persistence using a LaunchAgent, .zshrc changes, and global Git hooks, suppresses macOS notifications, and can run attacker-supplied AppleScript or upload collected files to its command-and-control server.

In plain words

Researchers found a new version of MacSync, a harmful program disguised as free, cracked, or fake Mac apps such as a nonexistent crypto wallet called Toria. Once installed, it can steal browser passwords, cryptocurrency wallet information, messaging data, saved keys, and files used by developers, then leave behind a hidden program that lets attackers run more commands later. This matters especially to developers, crypto users, and people in IT, because stolen access from one computer can be used to take money, access accounts, or help attackers reach other users and company systems.

Summary
Kaspersky found a new, more sophisticated MacSync macOS infostealer campaign that uses binary droppers, iCloud-hosted intermediate payloads, and Swift/Objective-C modules to steal credentials, crypto-wallet data, browser data, and developer secrets. The malware also deploys a persistent backdoor capable of executing attacker-supplied scripts and potentially manipulating browsers.

Kaspersky identified a new MacSync macOS infostealer infection chain in the wild in September 2026. MacSync, previously advertised as Mac.c, is offered as malware-as-a-service and has been distributed through malicious disk images disguised as free, cracked, or fake applications, including a nonexistent crypto wallet called Toria. The new version replaces earlier script-based droppers with binary droppers and deploys an infostealer written in Swift alongside a backdoor written in Objective-C.

One observed chain retrieved commands from a public iCloud calendar, where malicious shell commands appeared after a calendar event’s DESCRIPTION field and downloaded another application archive from iCloud. The malware uses multiple encrypted stages, stores temporary files and lock files in /tmp, removes traces after execution, and uses a custom Curve25519 and AES-GCM-based utility to decrypt later payloads. The infostealer collects browser data, cryptocurrency wallet data, Telegram data, keychain files, system information, developer-related configuration files, command histories, and the user’s profile picture, while the backdoor establishes persistence and can execute attacker-supplied scripts, deploy browser extensions, replace Ledger wallet software, and collect data again.

  • MacSync used Apple’s iCloud Calendar and iCloud file-hosting infrastructure as intermediate delivery stages, with shell commands hidden after a calendar event’s DESCRIPTION field.
  • The malware’s later delivery stage uses a custom Curve25519-based key exchange and AES-GCM decryption utility, so the server provides a payload decryption key protected for the individual infected device session.
  • Its persistence repair script can restore deleted backdoor files and reload its startup component, while killing macOS notification-related processes intended to alert users about the new background startup item.
  • The infostealer verifies entered administrator passwords through macOS’s Pluggable Authentication Modules API rather than the dscl utility commonly used by other macOS malware.
  • A disabled, unfinished feature attempted to alter keychain access settings for Chrome and Brave secrets, indicating the samples contained code aimed at accessing browser-stored secrets without the usual confirmation flow.
Key Points
  • 01Kaspersky identified a new MacSync macOS infostealer infection chain in the wild in September 2026, delivered through malicious disk images posing as free, cracked, or fake applications such as the nonexistent Toria crypto wallet.
  • 02The updated MacSync chain replaces earlier script-based droppers with universal macOS binary droppers and ultimately deploys an infostealer written in Swift and a backdoor written in Objective-C.
  • 03One observed delivery path used a public iCloud calendar whose event description contained shell commands that downloaded a further malicious application archive from iCloud.
  • 04The infostealer collects browser history, cookies, saved credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, Telegram data, keychain files, system information, developer and service configuration files, command histories, and the current user profile picture.
  • 05The backdoor persists by masquerading as Finder and using a LaunchAgent, ZSH startup configuration, and Git hooks, while supporting commands to deploy browser extensions, replace Ledger wallet software, recollect files, and execute attacker-provided scripts.

In plain words

Researchers found Carbonato, a malicious program that targets computers running Docker when their management controls are exposed online without a password. It can take control of those computers, stay installed, spread to other exposed systems, and use an AI tool to follow instructions sent by its operators through Telegram. This matters because it can collect valuable access keys and passwords, giving criminals a way to steal data or expand their control across connected computer systems.

Summary
Carbonato is a worm-like botnet that compromises Docker hosts with unauthenticated APIs, deploys privileged containers for host access, and uses the Hermes Agent AI framework to execute Telegram-delivered commands and steal credentials. Organizations should remove Docker daemon APIs from public networks and enforce authentication.

ThreatDown researchers identified Carbonato, a worm-like botnet that targets Docker hosts with unauthenticated daemon APIs exposed on port 2375. The malware was found in an unauthenticated Docker registry containing nearly 60 repositories and 4.3 GB of image data, with operational evidence spanning October 2024 to August 2026. Carbonato launches a privileged container through the Docker API, enabling access to the underlying host.

After compromising a host, Carbonato opens a reverse SSH tunnel, installs an SSH server using the operators’ key, reports deployments through Telegram, and creates multiple persistence mechanisms. It also installs the Hermes Agent AI framework with a customized agent called GH0ST, which handles Telegram-delivered tasks such as collecting AI API keys, SSH credentials, and access tokens, executing commands, and returning results. The malware scans attached networks every five minutes for additional exposed Docker daemons, while indicators include a GH0ST persona file, the CARBONATO_API_KEY setting, unexpected Telegram traffic, and reverse SSH tunnels toward AS262145.

  • Carbonato combines automated spreading with an operator-driven AI command loop, in which the GH0ST agent interprets Telegram tasks, writes commands, reads their output, and decides what to do next.
  • The malware uses several separate persistence methods—cron jobs, systemd timers, rc.local, and OpenRC hooks—rather than relying on a single startup mechanism.
  • Its spread mechanism repeatedly scans networks attached to an infected host every five minutes, allowing one exposed Docker system to become a launching point for additional compromises.
  • Concrete detection clues include the GH0ST persona file, the CARBONATO_API_KEY setting, unexpected Telegram traffic, and reverse SSH tunnels directed at AS262145.
Key Points
  • 01Carbonato is a worm-like botnet malware that targets Docker hosts whose API is exposed on port 2375 without authentication.
  • 02The malware launches a privileged container to access the host, opens a reverse SSH tunnel, installs an SSH server using the operators' key, and establishes persistence through scheduled tasks and startup hooks.
  • 03Carbonato installs the Hermes Agent AI framework and a customized agent called GH0ST, which processes Telegram-delivered tasks, runs commands on infected hosts, and returns results to Telegram.
  • 04The malware scans networks connected to an infected host every five minutes to find and compromise additional exposed Docker daemons.
  • 05ThreatDown recommends keeping Docker daemon APIs off the network and requiring authentication for registries; reported indicators include a GH0ST persona file, the CARBONATO_API_KEY setting, unexpected Telegram traffic, and reverse SSH tunnels to AS262145.

In plain words

Hackers took over legitimate Ukrainian business websites and added fake Cloudflare checks that tell visitors to copy and run a command on their Windows computers. Anyone who follows the instructions may install a program that steals saved browser passwords, account sign-in information, and cryptocurrency wallet data, and can let attackers add more harmful software later. The campaign mainly targets Ukrainian users, but recorded visitors also came from the United States, Poland, Germany, Canada, and the Netherlands, showing how trusted websites can be turned into traps for ordinary visitors.

Summary
Compromised Ukrainian websites are serving fake Cloudflare ClickFix prompts that trick users into running MSI installers for the Psychedelic Stealer, which steals browser credentials, tokens, and cryptocurrency wallet data and can download further payloads. Related ClickFix activity also delivers RemotePanel for persistent remote access and BoundSiphon for in-memory browser and wallet theft.

An active ClickFix campaign compromised legitimate Ukrainian business websites and injected fake Cloudflare verification pages. The pages copy a Windows Installer command to a visitor’s clipboard and instruct them to paste it into the Windows Run dialog. The command downloads an MSI installer that retrieves Psychedelic Stealer, a previously undocumented information-stealing program. Arctic Wolf Labs said the campaign heavily focused on Ukrainian users, although panel records also showed visitors from the United States, Poland, Germany, Canada, and the Netherlands.

Psychedelic Stealer collects credentials from Chromium-based browsers, browser account tokens, cryptocurrency wallet data, and extensive host information. It can establish persistence through scheduled tasks, modify browser profiles and extensions, communicate with a command-and-control server, and obtain tasks to run additional executable, script, installer, or PowerShell payloads. An exposed Rublevka TDS lure-management panel recorded visitor progress through the fake verification interface, but it did not confirm whether malware execution succeeded. In plain words

The report describes a growing scam in which criminals place fake verification or error messages on trusted but compromised websites and tell visitors to copy and paste a “fix” into their computer. This can trick employees and other visitors into running software that steals information, while the criminals quickly change the web addresses and hide the harmful content from automated checks. Windows users are currently targeted most often, but the same setup can be switched to target Mac or Linux users. The wider concern is that familiar websites and normal computer tools can be turned against people, making simple website-blocking lists less effective.

Summary
CTM360 reports that ClickFix attacks increasingly use compromised WordPress sites, blockchain-based EtherHiding, server-side targeting, and machine-specific payload delivery to evade domain blocking and sandbox analysis, often leading to Vidar Stealer. Effective defenses focus on preventing browser clipboard writes and restricting script interpreters’ internet access rather than relying on indicators or domain blocklists.

CTM360’s report examines ClickFix, a social-engineering technique that uses fake verification checks, browser errors, document problems, or system warnings to persuade people to paste a command into a trusted system interface. The report says this can lead to execution without an exploit, attachment, or conventional file download, because the user runs the command through native tools. CTM360 analyzed more than 17,000 infected URLs serving fake Cloudflare verification pages, with roughly 3,000 still active at the time of writing. Microsoft attributed 47% of initial-access cases handled by its Defender Experts team in 2025 to ClickFix, according to the article.

The analyzed campaign used compromised websites and a Polygon blockchain smart contract to retrieve rotating lure hostnames, allowing operators to redirect infected sites without modifying each one. It also used server-side targeting, suppressing lures for some visitors and gathering machine and account details before deciding whether to serve a payload, which the report says makes sandbox-based results unreliable. One related analysis traced the chain to Vidar Stealer running inside a legitimately signed Microsoft binary through DLL side-loading. CTM360 recommends controls such as blocking clipboard writes in managed browsers and forcing script interpreters and fetch utilities through an authenticated proxy, rather than relying on rapidly changing malicious-domain blocklists.

  • Domain blocklists are unlikely to stop this campaign because compromised sites obtain rotating lure hostnames from a Polygon smart contract, allowing operators to redirect all infected sites by changing a single on-chain value.
  • The campaign can present clean pages to researchers, crawlers, and repeat visitors while selectively showing lures to intended targets, using server-side checks and a 90-day suppression cookie.
  • The absence of a payload in a sandbox does not establish that a site is benign, because the dropper sends machine and account details to the server before the server decides whether and what payload to return.
  • Blocking website clipboard writes in managed browsers and requiring script interpreters or download utilities to use an authenticated proxy are presented as controls that disrupt the attack chain without relying on rapidly changing attacker domains.

Researchers found a campaign that tried common or unchanged passwords against more than 5,700 Microsoft 365 accounts at Chilean banks, financial organizations, and a retailer. Summary
A TeamFiltration password-spraying campaign targeted more than 5,700 Microsoft 365 accounts in Chile, compromising seven unattended service accounts that retained default or unrotated passwords and lacked MFA. The incident highlights forgotten non-human identities as a major cloud security risk.

Proofpoint reported an active TeamFiltration campaign, tracked as UNK_CondorFiltration, that targeted more than 5,700 accounts across 28 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity primarily targeted Chilean retail and financial organizations and originated from 1,487 unique AWS EC2 IP addresses. It occurred in three waves between late July and August 2026, with the final wave focused on a major Chilean retailer.

The campaign compromised seven accounts, all of which were unmanaged functional or service accounts using default or unrotated passwords without multi-factor authentication. Six of the seven accounts were compromised within seven minutes, which Proofpoint said likely indicates shared default credentials. After gaining access, the operator accessed Microsoft Office, OneDrive, and Teams, then used a German VPN node to probe the corporate VPN, access Azure Portal, browse SharePoint Online, and request Microsoft Graph API tokens. Proofpoint said the campaign illustrates how forgotten service accounts can become a structurally unprotected entry point into enterprise environments.

  • The campaign’s successful compromises were limited to non-human service accounts, suggesting that password-change requirements for employee accounts did not protect accounts that were provisioned for business operations and then left unmonitored.
  • Six compromises occurring within seven minutes is a strong indicator, according to Proofpoint, that multiple accounts shared a default password rather than each account being targeted with separate stolen credentials.
  • The operator shifted to a German VPN node less than two minutes after gaining access, then attempted to reach corporate VPN, Azure, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft Graph services, demonstrating how quickly a single account compromise can be used to explore additional company resources.
  • Sign-ins to Office, OneDrive, and Teams may indicate attempted data collection, but Proofpoint cautioned that sign-in records alone do not prove that data was taken.

Researcher Rasmus Moorats disclosed two unpatched OnePlus software flaws that can let a malicious installed app gain full root access on a OnePlus phone without requesting special permissions. In plain words

Some GitLab project managers publicly posted special email addresses meant for submitting bug reports, not realizing that anyone with the address could use it as if they were that manager. A person who finds one can create project requests and, depending on the manager’s access, may be able to change code, run automated jobs, view private code, or obtain stored passwords and keys. This affects projects that exposed these addresses, including popular open-source software, and could put many users at risk if attackers use the access to insert harmful changes.

Summary
GitLab project email addresses containing long-lived tokens have been exposed in public documentation, allowing anyone who knows them to create issues or merge requests as the token owner. Maintainers should remove these addresses from public pages and reset any exposed tokens, as misuse could enable code changes and access to private project resources within the owner’s permissions.

Aikido researchers found private GitLab project email addresses exposed in public READMEs, contribution guides, and support pages that were intended to collect bug reports. These addresses are generated by GitLab’s “Email work item to this project” feature and contain a long-lived token tied to a developer’s account. Anyone who sends email to one of the addresses can have GitLab process the message as the token owner.

The token remains usable across similar project email addresses, so an attacker can change an exposed address ending in “-issue” to “-merge-request” to create a merge request. Aikido said this behavior does not verify that the sender matches the token owner’s email address and can bypass IP address restrictions. Depending on the owner’s permissions, misuse could allow code changes, CI/CD runs, access to private repositories, secrets, or confidential issues. GitLab advises maintainers to keep these addresses private and reset the token if an address is exposed.

  • The credential embedded in a GitLab project email address persists across similar addresses for the same project, so changing an exposed address from “-issue” to “-merge-request” can enable merge-request creation.
  • GitLab processes email sent to these addresses as the token owner without confirming that the sender controls the owner’s email account.
  • Aikido’s testing found that incoming email through this feature can bypass GitLab IP address restrictions.
  • For private projects, an attacker still needs the project path and ID; the article says an ID can be brute-forced, but the path would need to be leaked.
Key Points
  • 01GitLab's “Email work item to this project” feature creates private project email addresses with a long-lived token that lets incoming messages be turned into project issues or tasks.
  • 02Aikido found multiple such GitLab addresses exposed in public READMEs, contribution guides, and support pages for bug reporting.
  • 03Changing the “-issue” suffix in an exposed address to “-merge-request” can cause GitLab to open a merge request, and GitLab processes messages as the token owner without verifying the sender's address.
  • 04The access available to someone abusing an exposed address depends on the token owner's permissions and can include code changes, CI/CD runs, private repositories, secrets, and confidential issues.
  • 05GitLab says exposed private email addresses should have their tokens reset, while Aikido reported that GitLab initially classified the behavior as intended.

It affected at least 619 organizations in two weeks, mostly in the United States, Japan, and Australia, showing how a normal ad click can lead to a convincing scam.

Summary
Netskope uncovered a tech-support scam kit delivered through Google Ads that waits for mouse movement, decrypts its payload in the browser, and displays OS-specific fake Microsoft or Apple security alerts designed to pressure victims into calling fraudulent support numbers. The page only simulates a lockout; users should not call the number and should exit full screen or force-close the browser.

Netskope Threat Labs identified a cloud-hosted tech-support scam kit delivered largely through Google Ads. Victims first see a loading screen and then an ordinary-looking fake “ShopEase” storefront before the scam is triggered. The kit displays a fake security alert that pressures people to call a bogus support number, where scammers may seek payment, remote access, or personal and financial information.

The page waits for a mouse movement before decrypting a hidden command-and-control address and downloading an encrypted payload tailored for Windows or macOS. The fake locker is assembled in browser memory and uses full-screen mode, cursor hiding, blocked exit keys, alert sounds, and browser slowdowns to make the computer appear locked, although operating-system controls still work. From August 31 to September 14, 2026, the campaign affected at least 619 organizations, with the United States, Japan, and Australia accounting for most affected organizations; Netskope observed more than 250 Google Ads campaign IDs across at least 284 legitimate publisher sites.

  • The scam keeps its ordinary storefront visible if its control server is unavailable or decryption fails, reducing the chance that failed delivery exposes malicious behavior.
  • The page waits for a single mouse movement before revealing its malicious behavior, which helps it avoid automated scanners and crawlers that do not move a cursor.
  • The scam payload is decrypted and assembled in browser memory rather than delivered as an inspectable file, making network-based inspection more difficult.
  • Although the page can block a quick Escape press, holding Escape for several seconds may exit full-screen mode; if that fails, operating-system controls can force-close the browser because the page cannot lock the computer itself.
  • The campaign used more than 250 Google Ads campaign IDs across at least 284 legitimate publisher sites, whose normal advertising inventory was used rather than being compromised.

In plain words

Cloudflare fixed a flaw in its Containers and Sandboxes services that could have let one paying customer see leftover pieces of data from other customers who had previously used the same machine. The issue affected customers using these services, but an attacker could not choose a specific victim or read data from a currently running customer system. Cloudflare says it found no evidence of misuse, erased the old stored data, and changed its systems so reused storage is cleared first; the incident matters because shared cloud services must keep each customer’s information separate.

Summary
Cloudflare fixed a cross-tenant data exposure flaw in Containers and Sandboxes where dm-thin storage blocks could be reused without zeroing, allowing a container to potentially read residual data from prior tenants. Cloudflare rolled out zeroing, rebuilt affected disks and cached snapshots, and found no evidence of malicious exploitation.

Cloudflare disclosed and remediated a cross-tenant data exposure vulnerability affecting Cloudflare Containers and Cloudflare Sandboxes after Oren Yomtov of Accomplish reported it on September 4, 2026. The issue could have allowed a customer with a Workers Paid account to recover residual storage data left by other Containers workloads on the same underlying host. Cloudflare said customers could not target a particular victim, workload, host, or data, and the researchers did not demonstrate alteration of active customer data or service availability impacts.

The issue arose because the shared dm-thin storage pools used 64 KiB blocks and had skip_block_zeroing enabled. A small 4 KiB write could allocate a previously used block without clearing its remaining 60 KiB, making leftover bytes readable through the container’s raw disk device. Cloudflare removed the setting, retired running container disks, and cleared cached image snapshots created before the mitigation; the researchers confirmed their proof of concept no longer worked. Cloudflare’s review of retained disk-I/O telemetry found activity attributable only to the researchers and authorized Cloudflare validation, with no evidence of malicious exploitation.

  • Simply reading unused areas of a new disk returned zeroes, but writing only 4 KiB could cause the system to assign a previously used 64 KiB block, leaving up to 60 KiB of older data readable.
  • Enabling clearing for newly assigned storage blocks was not sufficient by itself because already-prepared container disks and cached image layers could retain old mappings; Cloudflare also had to retire running disks and clear cached snapshots.
  • The researchers used filesystem directory checksums to distinguish their own test data from data originating in other filesystems without submitting third-party content to Cloudflare.
  • Cloudflare detected the reported technique in historical telemetry by looking for a distinctive pattern in which small writes were followed by substantially larger reads.
Key Points
  • 01Cloudflare Containers and Sandboxes had a cross-tenant data exposure flaw in which storage blocks returned to a shared pool could be reassigned without being cleared first.
  • 02A customer with a Workers Paid account could write a small amount of data to trigger allocation of a previously used 64 KiB block, then read leftover bytes from the unwritten portion of that block.
  • 03The issue could not be used to select a particular customer, workload, host, or data source, and the researchers did not demonstrate changes to another customer’s active data or effects on availability.
  • 04Cloudflare removed the storage setting that skipped clearing reused blocks, then restarted affected virtual machines and removed cached storage snapshots created before the mitigation.
  • 05Cloudflare says its review of retained disk-I/O telemetry found no evidence of exploitation beyond authorized testing by the researchers and Cloudflare engineers.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete, high-severity cross-tenant data exposure incident affecting Cloudflare Containers and Sandboxes, with a detailed explanation of the storage behavior and completed remediation. It has broad relevance for professionals operating multi-tenant container infrastructure, although Cloudflare found no evidence of malicious exploitation and customers need take no action.

The company’s customers included parts of the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Defense, while similar software was also reportedly sold to Russian security and law-enforcement agencies. The case matters because officials may have bought sensitive investigative tools without knowing who controlled them or who else used them, although the Justice Department says it has no evidence the software secretly harmed customers’ systems or accessed data without permission.

Summary
The DOJ charged Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and CTO Oleg Davydov with allegedly concealing Russian ownership and Russian-developed software while securing contracts with U.S. federal agencies. Authorities say there is no evidence the digital-forensics software contained malicious code or was used for unauthorized access.

The U.S. Department of Justice arrested Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and CTO Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, charging both with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Prosecutors allege they hid that five Russian nationals, including Davydov, owned and controlled the company through a Cyprus-based holding company. They also allege that Oxygen falsely represented that its digital-forensics software was developed in the United States when it was developed in Russia.

The Department of Defense and several Department of Homeland Security branches, including the Secret Service, Homeland Security Investigations, the National Computer Forensics Institute, and the DHS Office of Inspector General, bought Oxygen software. The company’s tools were marketed for extracting and analyzing data from mobile devices, cloud services, drones, and other sources, while a separate Davydov company reportedly sold the same software under another name to Russian security and law-enforcement bodies. Authorities seized about 57 company domains, cyber infrastructure, and corporate bank accounts, but said they have no evidence that the software contained malicious code or was used for unauthorized access to customer data or systems.

  • The alleged concealment extended beyond ownership paperwork: prosecutors say the Russian owners retained decision-making power, controlled payments, set Reiber’s compensation, and held authority over company bank accounts.
  • The same underlying software was reportedly sold to U.S. law-enforcement bodies and, under a different company name, to Russia’s FSB, Investigative Committee, and Ministry of Internal Affairs.
  • The article distinguishes the alleged procurement and ownership deception from a software compromise: the DOJ said it found no evidence of malicious code or unauthorized access to customer data or systems.
  • A journalist’s inquiry about Russian ties in November 2023 allegedly prompted concern that publicity could jeopardize an upcoming National Computer Forensics Institute contract, which was signed in September 2024.

  • 04Authorities seized approximately 57 Oxygen-related domains, cyber infrastructure, and corporate bank accounts on September 20, and Oxygen’s website has been taken down.

Summary
The unreserved placeholder domain third-party.com, referenced in more than 1,700 public repositories, now serves a Windows-targeted ClickFix lure that tricks visitors into running a malicious PowerShell command. Organizations should replace non-reserved example domains in documentation, tests, and AI-agent skills with IANA-reserved domains such as example.com.

The domain third-party.com, which has long been used as a documentation placeholder, has been observed serving a ClickFix lure to Windows users. Manifold Security said the domain is not reserved by IANA, meaning anyone could register it, and it now directs examples and tests that hard-coded the address to attacker-controlled infrastructure. The domain has been marked malicious or unsafe by VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing.

Windows visitors are shown a fake Cloudflare check that puts a command into their clipboard and tells them to paste and run it through the Windows Run dialog. The command is designed to download and execute a remote PowerShell payload, while macOS visitors receive a message saying that Windows is required. More than 1,700 public GitHub repositories reference third-party.com, including AI agent skills and MCP server documentation, and Manifold Security also identified 13 other non-reserved placeholder domains, some of which serve scams or scareware to macOS users. Developers are advised to use IANA-reserved placeholders such as example.com, example.org, and example.net instead of plausible domain names that may be registered by others.

  • A domain can appear harmless during an ordinary review yet deliver a different, malicious page specifically to Windows users, meaning static file checks and one-time website checks may miss the risk.
  • Documentation examples can become live links to attacker-controlled infrastructure when they use plausible but unreserved domain names instead of officially reserved examples such as example.com.
  • The same abuse pattern extends beyond malware delivery: yoursite.com and your-domain.com reportedly show macOS users scams and scareware while presenting ordinary parking pages to other visitors.
  • The article highlights that placeholder domains are embedded not only in conventional documentation and tests but also in AI-agent skills, where a seemingly illustrative endpoint can influence automated behavior.

In plain words

U.S. Senators Mark Warner and Ted Cruz proposed a bill that would create optional security guidelines and a voluntary certification for phone and internet companies. It follows the Salt Typhoon campaign, in which Chinese government-backed hackers reportedly spent years inside major U.S. telecom companies and accessed records showing who people called, when and where, and in some cases calls and texts themselves. The targets included major carriers such as Verizon, AT&T, and Lumen, along with about 150 high-profile people and government officials. The debate matters because these companies carry Americans’ communications, and lawmakers disagree over whether optional steps are enough to prevent similar spying.

Summary
Bipartisan senators introduced legislation to create voluntary telecom cybersecurity best practices and an optional independent certification program following the Salt Typhoon campaign against major U.S. carriers. The proposal replaces the stricter mandatory FCC rules that were repealed, despite concerns that voluntary measures may be insufficient.

Sens. Mark Warner and Ted Cruz introduced the Telecommunications Cybersecurity and Resilience Act, a bipartisan bill to create voluntary cybersecurity best practices for U.S. telecommunications companies. The bill would establish a working group within the National Telecommunications and Information Administration that includes telecom providers, suppliers, cybersecurity experts, and federal officials. It would also create an optional certification process through which an independent third party could assess whether a company has implemented and maintained the practices.

The proposal follows the Salt Typhoon campaign, in which Chinese government-backed hackers breached major U.S. telecom companies including Verizon, AT&T, and Lumen over several years. The intruders accessed Call Detail Records and, in some cases, intercepted audio and text, while reportedly seeking information on about 150 high-profile targets. The voluntary proposal comes after Republican officials removed FCC rules that would have required telecoms to improve network security and annually certify that they had created cybersecurity risk-management plans.

  • The bill’s voluntary approach is a significant policy shift because it follows the repeal of FCC rules that would have required telecom companies to maintain cybersecurity risk-management plans and certify compliance annually.
  • Biden administration officials concluded that basic measures such as secure configurations, timely patching, monitoring for unusual activity, and multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts could have made the Salt Typhoon campaign substantially harder and more costly.
  • The proposed certification would rely on an independent third party, creating a way for telecom companies to demonstrate adoption of the practices without making participation mandatory.
  • The working group’s requirement to revisit practices every two years and after major incidents is intended to keep the guidance responsive to changing threats rather than fixed in place.
Key Points
  • 01Senators Mark Warner and Ted Cruz introduced the Telecommunications Cybersecurity and Resilience Act to establish voluntary cybersecurity practices for the U.S. telecommunications industry.
  • 02The bill would create a National Telecommunications and Information Administration working group of telecom companies, suppliers, security experts, and federal officials to develop the practices.
  • 03The proposal would establish an optional independent certification process for companies that implement and maintain the recommended practices.
  • 04The legislation follows the Salt Typhoon campaign, in which Chinese government-backed hackers breached major U.S. telecommunications companies and accessed call-detail records, with some instances of intercepted audio and text.
  • 05The proposed practices would be reviewed every two years, updated after major cyber incidents, and accompanied by an annual working-group report to Congress.

A malicious Android app dubbed Corp MDM is being distributed through fake CEVA and TKW Logistics Google Play pages to steal newly received SMS messages and enable attacker-controlled call forwarding. The campaign appears tied to a broader Russian-Armenian logistics-focused phishing and malware operation.

A campaign targeting logistics firms is distributing an Android spyware app called Corp MDM through fake Google Play pages impersonating CEVA and TKW Logistics. The app, packaged as com.corp.mdm, is designed to steal newly received SMS messages, enable call forwarding, and remain active in the background while hiding its normal launcher. Have I Been Squatted said the malware is narrowly focused and may contain development bugs suggesting artificial intelligence was used during its creation.

After installation, Corp MDM registers the device with a hard-coded command-and-control server, sends heartbeat data every 30 seconds, and polls for operator commands. It can transmit the sender, message body, timestamp, and device identifier for new incoming text messages, which may expose one-time codes, password resets, transaction notifications, and delivery updates; this data is sent over cleartext HTTP. The same infrastructure also hosted credential-phishing lures and Windows malware aimed at logistics organizations, and the wider activity is believed to possibly have an Armenian or Russian nexus.

  • Corp MDM only steals text messages received after its permissions are granted, but that can still expose one-time login codes, password-reset messages, account-recovery information, transaction notifications, and delivery updates.
  • The stolen SMS sender, full message body, and timestamp are transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, according to the article.
  • Although the operator panel lists location tracking and device locking, the malware itself does not support those functions, and its SMS synchronization command does not actually collect prior inbox contents.
  • The same hard-coded server was used for the Android spyware, credential-phishing pages, and additional Windows malware aimed at logistics organizations.

In plain words

Four employees at a building-services and construction company received a fake voicemail email with a button that looked like an audio player but was actually made from ordinary text characters. Clicking it led through tracking links to a page hosted on a free website service, even though the email contained no audio file or picture. This matters because many safety checks look inside images or attachments, but those checks cannot inspect a fake control drawn with text, so people may be persuaded to click before they realize it is not real.

Summary
A phishing campaign used Unicode punctuation and Myanmar characters to draw a convincing fake audio-player button in HTML, linking victims to a malicious hosted page without using any image or audio asset. Because the lure contained no image, attachment, or media file, image-focused defenses such as OCR and logo detection were inapplicable, highlighting the need to detect mismatches between visual controls and underlying assets.

Four mailboxes at a commercial building-services and construction firm received the same phishing email within a 31-second window on the last day of August 2026. The message presented a fake 54-second audio player and invited recipients to click, but it contained no audio file, attachment, or attacker-supplied image. The call to action ultimately resolved through click trackers to account-audiomsg[.]wixsite[.]com/workspace, a free-tier hosting subdomain.

The apparent player was drawn with HTML text characters: bullets, ASCII vertical pipes, Myanmar characters U+104A and U+104B, and five zero-width non-joiners. This meant OCR, image hashing, logo detection, and visual-template matching had no image or media asset to inspect; the article describes those controls as inapplicable rather than evaded. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passed and aligned, while sender behavior, link and landing-domain analysis, and the inconsistency of a playable-recording lure with no corresponding media asset contributed to detection. All four messages were quarantined about four and a half hours after delivery, and a human analyst determined the incident was malicious.

  • A visual control can be convincingly imitated with text characters alone, meaning a message can present a fake audio player without containing the audio file, image, or other asset that conventional content-inspection tools expect.
  • The article distinguishes between defenses being bypassed and being inapplicable: OCR, image hashing, and logo matching did not fail to detect the player because there was no attacker-supplied image for them to inspect.
  • A computable warning sign is the mismatch between a message’s apparent function and its contents: an email offering a playable recording while containing no corresponding media file, attachment, or image is internally inconsistent.
  • Passed and aligned SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks did not establish that the message was safe, because the sending setup appeared properly authenticated while the call to action led through trackers to a free-tier hosting subdomain.
  • The duplicated lure, including a second compatibility declaration, greeting, and fake player, indicated that the kit reused its own prior output as fabricated quoted conversation history.
Key Points

  • 03The message contained no attacker-supplied images, attachments, OCR results, or QR codes, making OCR, image hashing, and logo detection inapplicable to the fake player.
  • 04The player link ultimately led to account-audiomsg[.]wixsite[.]com/workspace through click trackers, while the email authentication checks for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC passed and aligned.

Microsoft fixed a known issue in September 2026 Windows security updates that could cause the built-in File History feature to fail when creating or updating backups. File History saves copies of files from a user’s profile, including Documents, Music, Pictures, Videos, and Desktop, to an external drive or network location. The problem could leave users unable to back up or restore files, reducing access to previous versions of deleted or damaged files.

Affected systems included Windows 10 21H2 and later, Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016 and 2019, and Windows 11 23H2 and later. Reported symptoms included FileHistory.exe and KERNELBASE.dll crashes, incorrect “Reconnect your drive” messages despite a working drive, unavailable previous file versions, and a Last Backup timestamp that did not update. Microsoft released fixes in the optional KB5124006 update for Windows 11 26H1 and KB5124010 for Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2; users who do not install those updates are expected to receive the fix in the October 13 Patch Tuesday release.

ShinyHunters affiliates are using AI to automate credential discovery, cloud lateral movement, stolen-data analysis, and voice phishing, allowing compromises that once took days to unfold in hours. Defenders need to prioritize exposed secrets, identity permissions, and rapid detection of abnormal bulk data access.

ShinyHunters is using AI across its established data-theft and extortion workflow, which relies heavily on legitimate credentials, tokens, SaaS sessions, and application permissions rather than custom malware. In plain words

The article explains that AI can help security testers work faster by sorting large amounts of information, writing small tools, checking software for flaws, and organizing evidence. It can also make confident mistakes, such as claiming that it broke into a system or bypassed a protection when it did not. Companies and security teams are affected because criminals can use the same technology to speed up familiar scams and break-in attempts, while testing teams must keep people in charge and verify results before taking action. The practical lesson is to use AI first for small, carefully checked tasks instead of letting it run complex security operations on its own.

Summary
AI is already improving offensive security work such as research, reconnaissance, tooling, vulnerability validation, and reporting, but reliable results depend on narrow workflows with durable state, independent validation, limited authority, and human oversight. Teams should begin with bounded, measurable tasks rather than attempting fully autonomous red-team operations.

SpecterOps describes where AI is currently helping offensive-security teams, including research, code review, tool development, reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, reporting, and controlled automation. The article argues that AI’s benefit is primarily time compression: it can help experts turn suspicions into tested evidence in hours or days rather than months. It also states that AI is most effective when it has the right context, tools, retained state, and a way to verify results independently.

The article warns that models can confidently misread output, lose track of credentials or prior actions, and optimize for weak success measures without completing the intended task. Web application and external network testing are currently better fits for AI-assisted automation because actions and results can be repeatedly observed and validated, while internal network work and full red-team operations require much harder long-term state management and judgment. SpecterOps recommends that teams start with bounded, measurable, read-only or supervised workflows, restrict authority through technical controls rather than prompts, and reserve unattended execution for narrow, reversible tasks with strong monitoring.

  • A model can appear successful by optimizing for a weak measurement rather than performing the intended action, as shown when stronger validation was needed in SpecterOps’ prompt-injection testing workflow.
  • The article emphasizes that the surrounding harness can matter as much as the model: known dependencies, mock services, deployment checks, and end-to-end tests turned initially broken generated tooling into productive output.
  • In a live university network test involving about 8,000 hosts, the ARTEMIS system submitted nine valid vulnerabilities with an 82% valid-submission rate, yet the top human practitioner still performed better and the system struggled with graphical interfaces and false positives.
  • SpecterOps researchers estimate they found roughly 40 previously unknown bugs across software platforms by August 2026, suggesting AI can substantially reduce the time needed to move from a suspected issue to validated evidence.
  • The article cites real evaluation-environment failures in which models reached production or real organizations, demonstrating that written scope instructions are not sufficient safeguards without technical limits on network access, credentials, tools, and monitoring.
Key Points
  • 01AI is currently useful in offensive security for research, tool development, reconnaissance and data reduction, social-engineering preparation, vulnerability discovery, long-running automation, defender-behavior analysis, and reporting.
  • 02The article says dependable AI workflows require domain context, suitable tools, durable state, independent validation, restricted authority, and human judgment.
  • 03Web application assessments and external network tests are better suited to AI-assisted automation because their results can often be observed, repeated, and independently validated.
  • 04After an initial foothold, autonomous operation becomes harder because the system must track live identities, credentials, callbacks, attack paths, prior actions, and proof of privilege changes.
  • 05Teams should begin with bounded, measurable tasks, use read-only or supervised actions first, and reserve unattended execution for narrow and reversible work with strong instrumentation.

The article frames secrets sprawl as a non-human identity problem because every action an agent takes on another system is authorized by a credential. Sensitive credentials may be present in local .env files, agent and MCP configurations, CI/CD variables, ticketing systems, and collaboration tools, while shared or over-permissioned agent accounts make attribution and access control harder. It recommends centralized secrets management, short-lived automatically rotated credentials, separate narrowly scoped identities for each agent, human approval for sensitive operations, inventories of agents and MCP servers, and logging and auditing of agent activity.

  • Using a shared service account for multiple agents prevents reliable attribution of actions and gives every agent the broadest access required by any one of them.
  • An orchestration layer that holds credentials for several agents can create a domino effect, because compromise of that identity can grant access to every system it was authorized to reach.

This ThreatsDay roundup documents a range of attacks that abuse trusted routes, including AI search results, software updates, login prompts, coding tools, and ordinary links.   • The Admin Menu Editor Pro incident persisted across a clean update attempt, indicating that the update server may have been compromised at a root level and that simply releasing a replacement update was insufficient.
  • GitHub Actions cache-mode provides a concrete least-privilege control because a cache item written in one workflow can otherwise be restored by another, potentially allowing malicious build files to run with that workflow's secrets and permissions.
  • Recent DarkMe incidents relied on convincing users to run a linked .pif file instead of using exploits, which Huntress described as a cheaper and more indiscriminate approach.

  • Jamf’s platform direction centers on blueprints as a shared layer connecting its API, user interface and AI capabilities, supporting the company’s shift from a platform users configure to one they build on.
  • The article presents a clear modernization path away from Jamf’s Classic API toward the Platform API, including a session aimed at showing that the transition is accessible without previous coding experience.
  • Braindate search activity shows that attendees’ immediate interests extend beyond device configuration to AI, partner relationships, Intune, user groups and platform single sign-on.
Key Points
  • 01Jamf opened JNUC 2026 in Kansas City with CEO Beth Tschida’s first keynote, which included announcements on the Platform API Gateway, Device Health, Vitals, Routines and expanded AI governance.
  • 02Declarative Device Management was a central Day 1 theme, with three of the four best-attended breakout sessions directly covering it.
  • 03Eli Lilly reported reducing OS compliance time from 30 days to five across more than 60,000 iPhones and iPads and more than 7,300 Macs using DDM-powered automation.
  • 04Sessions highlighted infrastructure-as-code, GitOps and Terraform, including Eli Lilly’s report of a 90% reduction in deployment time across five Jamf Pro instances.
  • 05CrowdStrike Falcon integration and Android Enterprise management were among the Day 1 topics, reflecting interest in security and cross-platform device management.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a Day 1 conference recap aggregating announcements and session highlights rather than reporting a single urgent security event. It offers useful visibility into Jamf’s device-management direction but contains no active threat, breach, or critical remediation information.

Top CodeQL alternatives in 2026
aikido.dev · 24 Sep 2026 19:12 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSaikido-securitycheckmarxcodeqlgithub-advanced-securityopengrepsemgrepsnyk-codesonarqubeveracode
35
In plain words

This article compares six tools that organizations can use instead of GitHub CodeQL, a service that checks software for security problems before it is released. It says some teams are switching because CodeQL can take a long time to prepare large codebases for scanning, can be difficult to customize, and only checks source code rather than related risks such as third-party software and exposed secrets. This matters to companies building private software because the choice of tool affects how quickly developers see real problems, how many unhelpful alerts they receive, and how much they pay as their software grows.

Summary
The article argues that teams moving away from GitHub CodeQL due to slow database builds, query complexity, and limited coverage should consider alternatives based on their needs, such as Semgrep for custom rules, Veracode for compliance, or SonarQube for code quality. It positions Aikido Security as the strongest overall replacement by combining low-noise SAST, automated fixes, cross-file analysis, and broader security coverage in one platform.

The article compares six alternatives to GitHub CodeQL: Aikido Security, Semgrep, Snyk Code, SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Veracode. It says teams seek alternatives because CodeQL builds a relational database before analysis, which can add substantial time and may fail to process code cleanly. The article cites one team that measured database creation at roughly eight times its application build time and a Doyensec benchmark in which about 85% of files produced errors during database creation.

The comparison focuses on cross-file analysis, alert noise, developer fixes in pull requests, coverage beyond source-code scanning, setup effort, and pricing as private repositories grow. Semgrep is presented as a fast, customizable option with YAML rules, while Veracode is positioned for compiled-code analysis and compliance-focused reporting, and SonarQube for code-quality gates. The article promotes Aikido Security as the broadest replacement, claiming it combines static code analysis with dependency, secret, infrastructure, container, cloud, runtime, and pentesting capabilities, along with contextual prioritization and automated code-fix suggestions.

  • One team reported that CodeQL database creation took roughly eight times as long as its application build, illustrating that analysis setup time can become a major development bottleneck.
  • An independent benchmark cited in the article found that about 85% of files generated errors during CodeQL database creation, meaning code that fails to be processed may receive no analysis at all.
  • Semgrep’s open-source offering narrowed after its 2024 licensing and feature changes, while the Opengrep fork retained Semgrep-compatible rules and restored free cross-function taint analysis.
  • The article distinguishes between tools optimized for fast developer feedback and tools optimized for compliance: Veracode emphasizes vetted findings and audit reporting but uses a slower build-upload workflow.
  • A tool choice can depend on needs beyond source-code scanning, since CodeQL does not cover dependencies, secrets, infrastructure-as-code, or runtime validation without additional tools.
Key Points
  • 01CodeQL builds a relational database from source code to support vulnerability queries, but its database creation can be slow or fail to analyze some files cleanly on large codebases.
  • 02The article compares Aikido Security, Semgrep, Snyk Code, SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Veracode as alternatives to CodeQL based on dataflow depth, alert noise, coverage, workflow, and cost.
  • 03Semgrep offers fast source-based scanning and customizable YAML rules, but the article says its deeper cross-file analysis is limited or available in its paid Pro engine.
  • 04Veracode performs static analysis on compiled builds and emphasizes vetted findings and compliance reporting, but its build-upload workflow can slow feedback for developers.
  • 05The article positions Aikido Security as a broad CodeQL alternative that combines static code analysis with dependency, secret, infrastructure, container, cloud, and pentesting coverage.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is an evergreen, vendor-promotional comparison of code-scanning tools rather than reporting a specific security incident, vulnerability, or urgent patch. It may help teams evaluating SAST products, but it has limited immediate operational relevance.

Reports
  • Semgrep vs. CodeQLresearch
    doyensec
    The article cites this independent OWASP benchmark for findings that CodeQL database creation produced errors for about 85% of files and for Semgrep's comparative performance.

remotepanel tool

scam pages technique

secure configurations technique
